title: Priapism
subtitle: Ischaemic or not: the corporal gas decides

sources.org: American Urological Association (AUA) and Sexual Medicine Society of North America (SMSNA)
sources.title: Diagnosis and Management of Priapism: AUA/SMSNA Guideline
EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health: priapism

red_flags.text: A painful, rigid erection with soft glans lasting more than four hours: ischaemic priapism, a compartment syndrome of the penis.
Sickle cell disease or trait, haematological malignancy, or recent intracavernosal injection, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, antipsychotic, trazodone or recreational drug use.
Duration beyond 24 to 48 hours. The chance of preserving erectile function falls steeply with time, and the patient must be told so.
Cardiovascular disease or uncontrolled hypertension in a patient who will need intracavernosal sympathomimetics.

do_now.text: Take a focused history (duration, pain, trauma, drugs, sickle cell status) and aspirate corporal blood for a blood gas to distinguish ischaemic from non-ischaemic priapism.

Ischaemic priapism: perform a dorsal penile nerve block, then corporal aspiration with or without saline irrigation and intracavernosal injection of a diluted sympathomimetic (phenylephrine is the agent of choice), repeated as per guideline dosing.
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate during intracavernosal sympathomimetic treatment, with ECG monitoring in patients with cardiovascular risk.
In sickle cell disease, start the intracavernosal treatment above without delay; systemic sickle cell treatment runs alongside it, not instead of it.

assess.text: Ischaemic: rigid, painful, dark corporal blood. Non-ischaemic (arterial): partially rigid, painless, often after perineal or penile trauma, bright red corporal blood.
Stuttering priapism: recurrent self-limiting episodes. Each episode can progress to a full ischaemic event, so the patient needs a prevention plan.
Examine the abdomen, perineum and lymph nodes for an infiltrative cause.

investigate.text: Corporal blood gas. Ischaemic blood is hypoxic, hypercapnic and acidotic (EAU quotes pO2 under 30 mmHg, pCO2 over 60 mmHg, pH under 7.25); non-ischaemic blood resembles arterial blood.
Penile colour Doppler ultrasound to support the distinction and to locate an arterial fistula in non-ischaemic priapism, without delaying treatment of an ischaemic one.
Full blood count, reticulocytes and haemoglobin electrophoresis where sickle status is unknown; toxicology screen when relevant.

resuscitate.text: Analgesia and a penile block before aspiration; hydration, oxygen and haematology input for sickle cell crisis.

definitive.text: Ischaemic priapism that does not resolve with repeated aspiration and sympathomimetic injection: surgical corporoglanular (distal) shunt, then a proximal shunt if needed.
In prolonged ischaemic priapism with likely irreversible smooth muscle necrosis, discuss early penile prosthesis insertion with an experienced prosthetic surgeon.
Non-ischaemic priapism is not an emergency: initial observation is reasonable, with selective arterial embolisation if it persists and the patient wishes treatment.
Stuttering priapism: plan prevention with the patient and, where relevant, the haematology team.

escalate.text: Urology registrar on presentation for any erection lasting four hours or more.
Andrology or prosthetic surgery for failed shunts or prolonged ischaemia.
Haematology for sickle cell disease or suspected haematological malignancy.

notes: The corporal blood gas answers the question in minutes. Do it before ordering anything that will take longer.

Ischaemic priapism is a time-critical compartment syndrome. Counsel honestly about erectile dysfunction from the first conversation; it is often the outcome of delay that happened before the patient reached you.
Do not give intracavernosal sympathomimetics for non-ischaemic priapism. It is not ischaemic, and the treatment adds risk without benefit.
